rows.question: As a provider of a high-risk AI system, what do I have to put in the instructions for use I give to deployers?
rows.answer: Article 13(3) requires the instructions for use to state the identity and contact details of the provider and any authorised representative, the system's characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance, any pre-determined changes, the human oversight measures, the computational and hardware resources needed, the expected lifetime and maintenance measures including software updates, and how deployers can collect, store and interpret logs. The section on performance must cover the intended purpose, the declared accuracy metrics, robustness and cybersecurity, circumstances that could foreseeably lead to risks, any ability to explain outputs, performance for specific persons or groups, input data specifications, and the information deployers need to interpret outputs. Under Article 13(2), the instructions must be concise, complete, correct and clear, and supplied in a suitable digital or other format.

rows.question: Under Article 13, does the instructions-for-use document need to mention logging and human oversight?
rows.answer: Yes. Article 13(3) requires the instructions for use that accompany a high-risk AI system to cover both topics. Under Article 13(3)(d), they must set out the human oversight measures, including the technical measures that help deployers interpret the system's outputs. Under Article 13(3)(f), they must describe the mechanisms built into the system that let deployers properly collect, store and interpret the logs. The other required contents are. The provider's identity and contact details. The system's characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance. Any changes the provider decided in advance. The computational and hardware resources needed, the expected lifetime and the maintenance measures. The human oversight item always applies. The logging item applies only "where relevant".

rows.question: Which sectors does Annex III cover, and is a clinical decision-support AI in a hospital one of them?
rows.answer: Annex III covers eight areas: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and workers' management, access to essential private and public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management, and administration of justice and democratic processes. No, a hospital clinical decision-support AI is not an Annex III area. Healthcare appears only in specific use cases: eligibility for public healthcare services under Annex III(5)(a), life and health insurance pricing under Annex III(5)(c), and emergency patient triage under Annex III(5)(d). The system is still high-risk under Article 6(1) where it is, or is a safety component of, a medical device that needs third-party conformity assessment by a notified body under the Medical Device Regulation, which typically applies to Class IIa devices and above.

rows.question: Does Annex III include healthcare as a high-risk area?
rows.answer: Annex III lists high-risk AI systems under eight numbered areas: biometrics, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits; law enforcement, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law; migration, asylum and border control management, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law; and administration of justice and democratic processes. Healthcare decision making is not one of them: Annex III places healthcare at point 5(a), which covers AI systems intended to be used by public authorities or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them, and at point 5(d), which covers emergency healthcare patient triage systems. Health also appears in Annex III at point 5(c), risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance, and at point 7(b), a health risk posed by a person entering a Member State, and neither of those concerns healthcare decisions. Only a use case listed in Annex III makes a system high-risk on this route, so operating in an area is not enough on its own.

rows.question: Could the Commission add a brand-new area to Annex III through a delegated act?
rows.answer: Yes, but only within the limits Article 7 sets. Under Article 7(1) the Commission may adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 to amend Annex III by adding or modifying use cases of high-risk AI systems where both of the following conditions are fulfilled: the AI systems are intended to be used in any of the areas already listed in Annex III, and they pose a risk of harm to health and safety, or an adverse impact on fundamental rights, that is equivalent to or greater than the risk of harm or adverse impact posed by the high-risk AI systems already referred to in Annex III. Both conditions are cumulative, so a use case outside the existing areas cannot be added by delegated act; Article 7(2) lists the criteria for assessing that risk, and Article 7(3) allows a use case to be removed from Annex III where it no longer poses a significant risk and the overall level of protection is not reduced. Before adopting the delegated act the Commission must consult experts designated by each Member State (Article 97(4)), and the act enters into force only if neither the European Parliament nor the Council objects within three months of notification, a period extended by three months at the initiative of either of them, or earlier where both inform the Commission that they will not object (Article 97(6)).

rows.question: What procedure applies when the Commission wants to update the list of high-risk use cases?
rows.answer: Article 7 lets the Commission update the list of high-risk use cases in Annex III through delegated acts. It may add or modify a use case only where both conditions in Article 7(1) are met: the system is intended for use in an area already listed in Annex III, and its risk to health, safety or fundamental rights is equivalent to or greater than that of existing Annex III systems. It may remove a use case under Article 7(3) only where the system no longer poses significant risks and the deletion does not lower overall protection. Under Article 97, the Commission must first consult experts designated by each Member State and then notify the European Parliament and the Council. The act enters into force only if neither objects within three months, a period that can be extended by three months.

rows.question: I'm a musician and use an AI tool to create backing vocals for my album. Do I have to label the tracks as AI-generated?
rows.answer: No, the musician does not have to put a machine-readable label on the tracks, because marking under Article 50(2) is the provider's duty. Article 50(2) requires the provider of the AI tool to mark synthetic audio output in a machine-readable format so that it is detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. The musician uses the tool for professional activity, so the musician is a deployer under Article 3(4), which excludes only personal non-professional use. A disclosure duty can still arise under Article 50(4). It applies where the backing vocals are a deep fake, meaning generated audio that appreciably resembles an existing person's voice and would falsely appear authentic. In that case the deployer must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. Because an album is an evidently artistic and creative work, Article 50(4) only limits this duty and does not remove it. The deployer must disclose that such content exists in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work, for example in the album credits or liner notes.

rows.question: Does the AI Act require me to watermark an AI-generated short film I am releasing as a fiction piece?
rows.answer: Making AI-generated video does not by itself put a marking duty on the person who made it: the Article 50(2) duty to mark outputs in a machine-readable format and make them detectable as artificially generated belongs to the provider of the system. A person using the system is a deployer under Article 3(4) only where the use is not in the course of a personal non-professional activity, and the Act does not apply to the obligations of a natural person using an AI system in the course of a purely personal non-professional activity (Article 2(10)); a person who develops the system, or has it developed, and puts it into service for their own use under their own name or trademark is also its provider (Article 3(3) and Article 3(11)) and so bears that marking duty. Where the video is a deep fake, meaning AI-generated or manipulated content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful (Article 3(60)), the deployer must disclose that it has been artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(4)), and where it forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work that duty is limited to disclosing the existence of the generated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work. The information must be clear and distinguishable, given at the latest at the time of first exposure and accessible (Article 50(5)), and these duties apply from 2 August 2026.

rows.question: In the AI Act's high-risk list, what is the difference between an area and a use case?
rows.answer: Under Article 6(2), the AI systems referred to in Annex III are high-risk, and Annex III lists them under eight numbered area headings: biometrics; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control management; and administration of justice and democratic processes. An area is one of those eight numbered headings. A use case is a specific intended use listed within an area: in seven of the areas the uses are set out as lettered points, and for critical infrastructure the heading itself states the use, AI systems intended to be used as safety components in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or in the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity. Eight areas therefore exist, and a system is high-risk under Article 6(2) only where it matches a listed use case, so operating within an area is not enough on its own.

rows.question: How many high-risk areas does Annex III define?
rows.answer: Annex III defines eight high-risk areas: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment, workers' management and access to self-employment, access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Each area contains one or more specific use cases, and only a system that falls within a listed use case is high-risk under Article 6(2), which classifies the AI systems referred to in Annex III as high-risk.

rows.question: Why does the AI Act have an annex listing EU large-scale IT systems like SIS and Eurodac?
rows.answer: Annex X exists so that Article 111(1) can pick out the AI systems that get a special transitional regime. Annex X imposes no obligation of its own. It lists the Union legislative acts establishing large-scale IT systems in the area of freedom, security and justice, such as the Schengen Information System, Eurodac and the interoperability framework. Under Article 111(1), AI systems that are components of those systems and were placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2027 must be brought into compliance by 31 December 2030, without prejudice to the Article 5 prohibitions, and the Regulation's requirements must be taken into account in each system's evaluation and whenever its founding act is replaced or amended.

rows.question: When do AI systems inside the Schengen Information System have to comply with the AI Act?
rows.answer: Under Article 111(1), AI systems that are components of the Schengen Information System, one of the large-scale IT systems listed in Annex X(1), must be brought into compliance with the Regulation by 31 December 2030 if they were placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2027. SIS components placed on the market or put into service on or after 2 August 2027 get no transitional period and must comply from that point. In either case, the ban on prohibited practices has applied to them since 2 February 2025, and the Act's requirements must also be taken into account whenever SIS is evaluated, replaced or amended under its own legislation.

rows.question: Is there a minimal-risk tier in the AI Act, and what obligations apply to it?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act does not establish a formal minimal-risk category; minimal risk is descriptive shorthand for the residual class of systems that are neither prohibited under Article 5, nor high-risk under Article 6 (a safety component of, or itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment, or an Annex III use case), nor subject to the Article 50 transparency duties, nor general-purpose AI models. They have no mandatory obligations under the Chapter III high-risk regime, but their providers and deployers remain subject to Article 4 AI literacy duties and may adopt voluntary codes of conduct under Article 95.

rows.question: My company's spam filter uses AI. Which AI Act obligations apply to it?
rows.answer: The operator's company's AI spam filter is minimal risk. It isn't a prohibited practice, it isn't high-risk, and it doesn't trigger any of the transparency duties. So the Act places no mandatory obligations on the filter itself. Article 4 still applies. As provider or deployer, the company must take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among staff and others who deal with the system on its behalf. Those measures should take account of their technical knowledge, experience, education, training and the context of use. Article 95 is voluntary. It encourages providers and deployers of non-high-risk AI systems to adopt codes of conduct that apply some or all of the high-risk requirements to their systems.

rows.question: How does the AI Act distinguish a provider from a deployer?
rows.answer: Article 3 defines 68 terms used in the Regulation, including 'AI system' (machine-based, varying autonomy, possibly adaptive, inferring from input how to generate output influencing physical/virtual environments), 'provider', 'deployer', 'placing on the market', 'putting into service', 'substantial modification', 'general-purpose AI model', 'general-purpose AI system', 'systemic risk'.

rows.question: We bought an AI recruitment tool and rebranded it under our name. Do we become its provider?
rows.answer: Yes, the rebranding makes the operator the provider. Under Article 25(1)(a), any distributor, importer, deployer or other third party that puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service becomes its provider. It then takes on all provider obligations under Article 16, unless contractual arrangements allocate those obligations otherwise. A recruitment tool counts as a high-risk AI system because Annex III(4)(a) lists AI systems used to recruit or select natural persons, including placing targeted job advertisements, analysing and filtering applications, and evaluating candidates.

rows.question: Can an employer use webcams with AI to detect whether call-centre staff are frustrated or stressed?
rows.answer: No. Article 5(1)(f) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service or using AI systems that infer the emotions of a natural person in the workplace. A webcam system that detects frustration or stress in call-centre staff from facial biometric data is exactly that kind of practice, so it is prohibited. The only exception is a system intended for medical or safety reasons, and that exception is narrow. Monitoring staff for performance, productivity or customer-service quality does not meet it. If the employer's real purpose were medical or safety-related, the system would fall outside the prohibition. It would still be high-risk, because emotion recognition is listed in Annex III(1)(c). The deployer would also have to tell the exposed staff that the system is operating under Article 50(3), and process their personal data under Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680, as applicable.

rows.question: Is AI-based monitoring of employee fatigue for safety reasons allowed under Article 5?
rows.answer: Yes, fatigue monitoring for safety reasons is allowed under Article 5. Article 5(1)(f) prohibits AI systems that infer the emotions of a natural person in the workplace, but it exempts systems intended to be put in place or into the market for medical or safety reasons. Fatigue is also a physical state rather than an emotion, so fatigue detection to prevent accidents falls outside the prohibition.

rows.question: Would an AI module that controls a surgical robot's movements be a high-risk AI system?
rows.answer: Yes. An AI module that controls a surgical robot's movements is a high-risk AI system under Article 6(1). That provision applies when two conditions are met. First, the AI system is a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I. Annex I includes the Medical Device Regulation. Second, that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment. A surgical robot is typically a Class IIb or Class III medical device under the Medical Device Regulation, so a notified body must assess it, and the motion-control module is a safety component of it.

rows.question: Is AI software that is itself a medical device classified as high-risk under the AI Act?
rows.answer: Yes, but only where the medical device must undergo a third-party conformity assessment. Under Article 6(1), an AI system is high-risk when two conditions are both met: it is itself a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation before it is placed on the market or put into service. Annex I(11) lists the Medical Device Regulation (EU) 2017/745 and Annex I(12) lists the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (EU) 2017/746. Under the Medical Device Regulation, Class I software certifies itself without a notified body, so the Article 6(1) route does not apply. Software in Class IIa, IIb or III needs a notified body, so it is high-risk.
